newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed pledges Russia will pull out from Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Lebed pledges Russia will pull out from Chechnya.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed said on Tuesday that Moscow would push ahead with a planned troop withdrawal from Chechnya which was suspended last week.

Russian news agencies quoted Lebed as saying after talks in the breakaway region with separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev that both sides had reconfirmed their commitment to a peace deal last month which set out terms for the withdrawal.

"We are continuing to move towards a durable, long and perhaps everlasting peace," Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as telling reporters in the village of Novye Atagi, 20 km (12 miles) south of the Chechen capital Grozny.
Lebed, who is President Boris Yeltsin's personal envoy to Chechnya, flew to the mountainous southern region on Tuesday to try to shore up the August 31 peace deal after signs of strains.
The deal, which includes a five-year deferral of the question of Chechnya's future status, is intended to halt a 21-month-old conflict which has killed tens of thousands.

Lebed said he and Yandarbiyev had agreed to push ahead with the "demilitarisation" of Grozny under the deal and agreed in principle on the formation of a coalition government in Chechnya -- one of the potential sticking points.
"There are no differences in principle between the federal side and the Chechen opposition on the formation of a coalition government," Interfax quoted Lebed as saying.
An initial meeting to discuss the formation of the new government last week was boycotted by Chechnya's pro-Moscow leadership which says it is too early to talk about a coalition.

Lebed had held talks earlier on Tuesday with General Vyacheslav Tikhomirov, the Russian army commander in the region who suspended the withdrawal foreseen by the peace deal, citing a dispute over exchanging prisoners.

En route to Chechnya, Lebed said he was unlikely to join rebel commander Aslan Maskhadov at a meeting of the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly in Strasbourg on September 23 because the separatists' Islamic legal code did not respect human rights.
Lebed dismissed rumours of an imminent attack on Grozny by forces loyal to pro-Moscow Chechen leader Doku Zavgayev.
But he told Interfax that such talk showed the urgency of bringing the factions together in a coalition to avoid the mainly Moslem region collapsing into Afghan-style chaos.
An official of a largely pro-separatist assembly of Chechen political movements told Itar-Tass news agency his body had already set up a 20-member coalition cabinet.
Lebed said he would also discuss setting up a "joint commission" in the near future, whose job would be to administer federal funds to rebuild Chechnya after nearly two years of war.
The Russian military said a soldier had died overnight in one of three attacks on Russian positions in the region, but the night was otherwise calm.
An unnamed military official told Interfax the rebels were violating the peace deal by digging in in Grozny and training new recruits.
